newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian insurers must internationalise, ASIA says.
newsitem.headline: Asian insurers must internationalise, ASIA says.

text.p: Asia must become a major player in the international insurance market if it is to fulfil its potential as a key financial centre and reduce dependency on the West, a senior insurance executive said on Wednesday.

"Keeping premium dollars in Asia is part of the game, but the real game is to be a player," Philip Sherman, chief executive officer of Singapore's Asian Securitization and Infrastructure Pte Ltd (ASIA Ltd), told Reuters in an interview.
He said the region must have adequate insurance mechanisms to support the level of infrastructure investment in the region, much of which is provided by local financiers.
"Most of the capital needed in Asia already is here or will be generated here in Asia, the key is in the evolution of institutional structures so that things can be done (with it)," Sherman said.

"If you look at the amount of money that Asian central banks have invested in the Western world at short-term interest rates, that they basically borrow back back at higher prices, in a sense Asia is paying one to two per cent per annum for liquidity," he said.
The decision by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to create new regulations accommodating mono-line financial guarantee underwriting was a step forward, he said.
"Financial guarantees seem to be gaining acceptance in the market," he said.
Mono-line underwriters specialise in a specific risk area of insurance, writing no business outside that specialism.

Already a second financial guarantee insurer, The Global Guarantee Association, is being planned for launch, Sherman said, adding that the formation of guarantee insurers indicated Asia's growing sophistication.

But he said the process of evolution was not complete and to become true international players, local insurers "must be willing to offer, say, fire insurance in Germany because diversity is the key for insurance companies".

Asian insurers have been talking about the creation of an indigenous Asia-wide mega-reinsurer or international insurer for some time, but so far little has come of the discussion, which was renewed at last week's East Asian Insurance Congress conference in Singapore.
Opinions there differed as to the necessity of such companies and the impact that foreign international players would have, once licensed to underwrite locally.
Sherman said foreign competition would "greatly stimulate" Asia's insurance market as it had done in the banking sector.
A former merchant banker before taking up his post at ASIA Ltd, Sherman said:

"If you look at the local banks in Asia five or 10 years ago, they were quite old fashioned, moving at different speeds in different countries, but these institutions are rapidly changing their styles."
